chunks: What is an ISA?. The question: What is an instruction set architecture (ISA)?
The ISA (instruction set architecture) is the rulebook a processor offers to software.
It lists the instructions, how each is written in bits, the registers, how memory addresses work, and how interrupts and errors behave.
It is a contract: software depends only on the ISA, so the hardware inside can change.
Think of a restaurant menu. Customers order from the menu, and each dish has a fixed description.
The kitchen can change its stoves, staff and layout, as long as the dishes that arrive match the menu.
Likewise, a program written for an ISA runs on any chip that follows it, whether the chip is tiny or huge.
The ISA is the narrowest point in the stack.
Everything above it targets the contract; everything below can be rebuilt (pipelined, out-of-order, different cache sizes) as long as it honours the same behaviour.
Instruction: one basic command the processor understands, such as add. Register: a small fast storage spot named in the instruction.
Opcode: the part of an instruction's bits that says which operation it is. RISC / CISC: simple, regular instructions versus larger, more complex ones ("RISC vs CISC advantages").
Microarchitecture: the hardware design that carries out the ISA ("What is microarchitecture?")
In the RISC-V ISA, add x3, x1, x2 means "put x1 plus x2 into x3". It is stored as one 32-bit word, 0x002081B3 (the 0x means hexadecimal).
The word is made of fields: an opcode saying "register arithmetic", the destination register 3, the source registers 1 and 2, and a field that selects "add".
Change only that last field and the same word becomes sub , 0x402081B3.
The assembler (the tool that turns written instructions into bits) and every compliant chip agree on this layout. That is the whole idea: an ISA fixes meaning and bit layout.

"An ISA, or instruction set architecture, is the contract between software and a processor: the instructions and their encodings, the registers, data types, addressing modes, memory model and exception behaviour.
Software only depends on the ISA, so different microarchitectures can implement the same ISA and run the same binaries.
RISC ISAs like Arm and RISC-V use simple fixed-length load/store instructions, while CISC like x86 has variable-length, more complex ones. Examples are x86-64, Arm and RISC-V."
